project.name: treetracker-query-api
project.description: RESTful API that exposes Greenstand treetracker data (captures, planters, organizations, trees and more) for clients such as the web map app. It follows a Domain Driven Design layered architecture with Express protocol routers, a business model layer, and a knex/pg repository layer.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what treetracker-query-api is: a RESTful API that exposes Greenstand treetracker data such as captures, growers, organizations, and trees. It describes the project purpose, the development toolkit, and the setup steps, giving you a roadmap before you read any code. Use it to anchor the layered tour that follows: protocol/router, business model, and repository/infrastructure.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: server.ts is the runtime entry point. It loads environment configuration, starts the Express app listening on NODE_PORT, and cleanly destroys the knex connection pool on SIGINT. The actual Express application is built in app.ts, which registers global middleware, mounts every versioned resource router, and installs the global error handler. Together these two files define how the process boots and how a request enters the system.

tour.title: Runtime Configuration
tour.description: The app depends on a small set of runtime settings. The package.json manifest declares dependencies plus the build, lint, test, and start scripts, and points main at the compiled server/server.js. The .env.example template lists the environment variables the API expects at startup: the database connection URL, the database schema, and the log level that server.ts reads in Step 2.
tour.languageLesson: package.json scripts are the canonical entry points for a Node project. 'npm start' runs the compiled dist output, while 'main' tells consumers which file to load.

tour.title: Router Layer and Shared Utilities
tour.description: The router layer is the protocol boundary that app.ts mounts. routers/utils.ts is the most reused piece here: it provides an async handler wrapper, the global error handler that maps thrown errors to HTTP responses, and a shared query formatter. This is the plumbing every concrete router relies on to translate HTTP into model calls and back.
tour.languageLesson: The async handler wrapper is a common Express pattern: it wraps an async route so rejected promises forward to the error middleware instead of crashing the process.

tour.title: Concrete Resource Routers
tour.description: Building on the shared utilities from Step 4, the resource routers expose the API surface. treesRouter wires tree endpoints for filtered queries, counts, and featured trees. growerAccountsRouter exposes grower-account endpoints (count, featured, wallets, selfies, by id, list) and validates query parameters with Joi before delegating to the model layer. These routers show the repeating pattern used across all resources.

tour.title: Business Model Layer
tour.description: Between the routers and the database sits the business model layer, where domain rules live. Tree.ts orchestrates tree queries and counts across organization, date, tag, wallet, and geometry filters. GrowerAccount.ts curries a repository into use-case functions and builds HATEOAS links for paginated responses. The routers from Step 5 call directly into these models rather than touching the database themselves.
tour.languageLesson: Currying a repository into use-case functions (as GrowerAccount does) is functional dependency injection: the data source is bound once, leaving small single-purpose functions the router can call.

tour.title: Domain Model Contract
tour.description: The model and repository layers share a common typing contract. DbModel.ts is a base TypeScript interface with an index signature that every domain model interface extends, allowing arbitrary dynamic keys read straight from database rows. It is one of the most depended-upon files in the codebase, which is why it is worth understanding before the repositories that produce these rows.
tour.languageLesson: A TypeScript index signature ([key: string]: unknown) lets an interface accept arbitrary keys. It is a pragmatic escape hatch for shaping loosely-typed database rows into typed models.

tour.title: Repository Foundation
tour.description: The infrastructure layer talks to Postgres through knex. Session.ts, the single most depended-upon file in the project, wraps a knex connection and manages transaction begin, commit, and rollback state. BaseRepository.ts is the generic base that provides shared CRUD operations (getById, getByFilter, count, update, create) reused by every concrete repository. delegateRepository.ts is a factory helper that returns a function delegating a named model method to a repository instance, wiring models to data access.
tour.languageLesson: A generic BaseRepository<T> centralizes CRUD once and specializes per entity through the type parameter, so concrete repositories add only their entity-specific queries.

tour.title: Concrete Repository
tour.description: TreeRepositoryV2.ts shows how the foundation from Step 8 becomes real queries. It provides V2 tree lookups by id, organization, date range, tag, wallet, and featured selection, backing the Tree model from Step 6. This closes the loop: router to model to repository to database, the full path a tree request travels.

tour.title: Structured Error Handling
tour.description: Errors flow back up the same stack. HttpError.ts is a custom error class carrying an HTTP status code and a rollback flag. Repositories and models throw it, Session uses the rollback flag to decide transaction cleanup, and the global error handler in routers/utils.ts (Step 4) maps it to an HTTP response. This one small class ties the transaction, model, and protocol layers together.

tour.title: Containerization
tour.description: With the code understood, see how it ships. The Dockerfile is a single-stage build on node:16-alpine that installs dependencies with npm ci and runs the pre-built dist output via npm start, the same start script from Step 3. The tsconfig files drive the TypeScript compilation that produces that dist output before the image is built.
tour.languageLesson: This Dockerfile builds from pre-compiled dist output rather than compiling inside the image. A multi-stage build could instead compile in a builder stage, but keeping the build external keeps the runtime image minimal.

tour.title: Kubernetes Deployment
tour.description: The container from Step 11 runs on Kubernetes via Kustomize. deployment.yaml defines the Deployment, pinning the container to the DigitalOcean microservices node pool and injecting DATABASE_URL from a sealed secret, satisfying the env config from Step 3. kustomization.yaml is the base that aggregates the deployment, mapping, service, and sealed-secret manifests into one deployable resource set that overlays customize per environment.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize layers a base set of manifests with per-environment overlays, so prod and test share one base and change only what differs, avoiding manifest duplication.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: The capstone is automation. pull-request-ci.yml runs a clean install, TypeScript build, ESLint, and the full test and repository test suites on Node 20 for every pull request against main. deploy-prod-env.yml is a manually dispatched, approval-gated workflow that deploys a tagged release to the production Kubernetes cluster using the Kustomize overlays from Step 12, pinning the image to the npm package version. Together they show how code moves from a pull request to production.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions use 'on' triggers to run jobs. CI runs automatically on pull_request, while production deploy uses workflow_dispatch plus an approval environment so releases stay manual and audited.
